nominees.name: Hidetoshi Katori
nominees.affiliation: University of Tokyo and RIKEN, Japan

nominees.name: Jun Ye
nominees.affiliation: JILA, NIST and University of Colorado Boulder, USA

subfield: Atomic, molecular and optical physics; precision measurement
motivation: Katori proposed and first demonstrated the optical lattice clock: neutral atoms held in an optical lattice tuned to a 'magic' wavelength, where the trapping light shifts both clock states equally. This removes motion-induced and trap-induced shifts while many atoms are interrogated at once. Ye turned the concept into the most accurate and stable clocks ever built. His strontium lattice clocks reach systematic uncertainties near 10^-18, and his group has resolved the gravitational redshift across a millimetre-scale atomic sample. The idea is original and elegant, and it is completely general. It gives experimentalists an unprecedented level of control over atomic quantum states. These clocks are now driving the redefinition of the SI second and enabling relativistic geodesy. They are also used in searches for dark matter and for variation of the fundamental constants. Their influence reaches across physics, metrology and chemistry, and it will last.
